subject: OpsLyft SLO discussion — context-window, max token impact & next steps
messages:
From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>
To: Dana Rios <dana@opslyft.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 8 Aug 2027 15:04:00 -0700
Subject: OpsLyft SLO discussion — context-window, max token impact & next steps

Hi Dana — thanks again for the time earlier. Quick synthesis from our call and concrete asks so we stay aligned.

Summary of what OpsLyft needs (as I heard it):
- Primary flow: customer support assistant (multi-turn chat) with incremental streaming replies to the browser.
- Target latency goal: p95 perceived response (time-to-first-bytes / streaming start) around 300–500ms for short interactions (<512 input tokens).
- For long context sessions (history + long user prompt) we agreed the p95 target can rise; OpsLyft would like guidance on how output token limits and context window size will translate into latency.
- Concurrency baseline: initial PoC needs to support ~60 simultaneous active sessions, peak concurrency might reach 150 during demos/marketing spikes.
- Throughput: average of ~12 reqs/sec across the tenant, but bursts to ~120 reqs/sec.
- Streaming: required — browser should start receiving the first tokens as soon as they are generated (no blocking until full completion).

What we (Redwood) will deliver next:
1) A short SLO matrix showing p50/p95/p99 for three example prompt sizes (short: <512, medium: 512–2k, long: >2k) and expected latency delta when output tokens exceed 1k and 2k. Attachment: opslyft_slo_matrix.xlsx (stub).
2) A technical note on runtime behaviors that affect latency as context window grows (KV cache warmup, KV cache lookups, attention compute scaling, quantization implications). Attachment: redwood_latency_notes.pdf (stub).
3) Proposal for a canary configuration: smaller quantized model variant for fallback, streaming-first route, and a burst autoscale policy.

Requests for you:
- Please confirm the top 3 user flows you want prioritized for the PoC (chat, knowledge base lookup, and ticket summarization were called out) and share a small set of representative prompt lengths for each (avg input tokens, expected output tokens).
- If you have any current SLAs in procurement language (p95/p99 numbers), share those so our commercial can align.
- Are there any regulatory constraints or data-retention rules we should factor into Private/VPC deployment sizing?

Proposed timeline: PoC perf demo the week of Aug 23 — we can tune batch sizes and cache policies beforehand.

Thanks — attaching the two stubs referenced above and a short internal playbook we’ll use while sizing.

—
Ben Carter
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
ben@redwood.com
Attachment(s): opslyft_slo_matrix.xlsx (xlsx, 12KB stub), redwood_latency_notes.pdf (pdf, 48KB stub)

Ben — thanks for the clear recap. Confirming a few points and adding clarifications from our side: we absolutely need streaming to start delivering tokens so the UI shows progress quickly.

Prioritized flows for PoC (in order):
1) Live chat support (main priority) — typical inputs 50–400 tokens, outputs 20–200 tokens.
2) Knowledge lookups (search + short answer) — inputs ~200–800 tokens, outputs 50–250 tokens.
3) Ticket summarization (batch) — inputs up to 4k tokens, outputs 200–800 tokens (this can tolerate higher latency).

SLOs we want the vendor team to aim at for production:
- p95 time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for short chat turn: <= 500ms
- p99 overall generation latency for short chat turn: <= 1.2s
- For long summarization jobs, we can accept p95 up to 2s.

Notes: our legal team will share data-retention constraints separately (we have to retain transcripts for 6 months). Also we'll upload a sample prompt set to the shared Drive by EOD.

Happy to take the PoC week of Aug 23 — can you do a brief tech check on Aug 18?

Dana
Head of Platform Engineering, OpsLyft
dana@opslyft.com
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: OpsLyft SLO discussion — context-window, max token impact & next steps

Looping in some implementation notes so OpsLyft has visibility into tradeoffs before the tech-check:

Technical summary (draft):
- Cost / latency is roughly linear in output tokens and superlinear in sequence length for attention-bound models. Practically: doubling input+history length typically increases latency by ~1.6–2x depending on kernel efficiency and KV cache locality.
- Streaming helps perceived latency but does not avoid the total compute cost — it just spreads it out and allows earlier TTFB. If the model produces many small tokens (e.g., character-level), TTFB improves but total cost may increase slightly due to more iterations.
- KV cache warmup: the first request after a long pause can be slower; we'll recommend a warmup ping during canary.

Operational playbook suggestions (attachment: redwood_perf_playbook.md stub):
1) Canary profile: 10 concurrent sessions, two short-prompt templates, and one long-summarize job. Use canary to validate p95/TTR and p99.
2) Routing policy: prefer a quantized 8-bit variant for medium loads; fall back to full-fp16 model for high-quality long summaries. This reduces cost and improves cold-start latency for chat.
3) Autoscale: aggressive burst policy (scale up GPU pool within 30s) with circuit-breaker when GPU queue latency exceeds 800ms.
4) Token caps: apply soft limits at 3k input tokens for chat by default (with guardrail that returns a 'shorten prompt' suggestion). For summarization jobs, accept larger packs but route them to dedicated workers.

Questions for Ben/karthik:
- Can we get sample prompt distribution (percentiles for input/output token counts) prior to Aug 18 tech-check? That will let us generate more realistic p95 estimates.
- Karthik, can you draft the canary config (instance types + expected cost delta) and share a first-pass estimate?

Thanks — I’ll assemble the perf playbook and SLO matrix into a single deck for the PoC runbook.

—
Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com
Attachment(s): redwood_perf_playbook.md (markdown, 6KB stub)
